sparks.title: Burned-seed exclusivity for one-night buyers
sparks.mechanism: Design for a couple paying out of pocket tonight for a first-dance song or a family paying for a memorial video. The thing they need, and that mainstream tools ignore, is assurance that no one else will ever get the same output. A seller generates the piece, then a human signatory destroys the prompt, seed and stems on record and signs a certificate, with a refundable bond held in escrow against any near-duplicate appearing later. The money goes to whoever can credibly certify scarcity, and that makes exclusivity a priced product that also benefits brands and games buying assets.
sparks.whyNonObvious: Generative tools are sold on abundance, so nobody builds the opposite: paying a premium to guarantee that something will never be made again.
sparks.firstStep: Offer ten custom wedding songs at two prices, one standard and one with a signed destroyed-seed certificate and a $200 escrow bond, and record which one sells.

sparks.title: The data-center town as the hidden royalty recipient
sparks.mechanism: Remove the creative industry as the endpoint of the money. Part of a $10 music-generation subscription becomes a payment for electricity, grid capacity and land in places like Loudoun County or rural Ireland. Some of the money that once went as a session fee to a musician in Nashville now goes to a utility and a landowner several states away. Converting creative AI spend into kilowatt-hours and the tax receipts of specific counties shows a geographic transfer from creative cities to grid-rich towns.
sparks.whyNonObvious: People picture AI money stopping at the model company, and do not follow it through the compute bill to municipal budgets.
sparks.firstStep: Estimate the energy cost per generated three-minute song from published inference figures, then map which utilities and counties host the inference capacity of the two largest music generators.

sparks.title: One-person likeness trust with splits to collaborators
sparks.mechanism: Solve it for exactly one person, such as a dead football commentator whose voice is being revived. Every licensed use of the voice pays into a trust, and the trust deed splits income with the producers, writers and broadcast engineers whose work shaped that voice, not only the estate. The core survives at scale: a likeness ledger per person that sends money to the collaborators who built the persona, which current likeness deals cut out.
sparks.whyNonObvious: Likeness rights are treated as belonging to one face, but a famous voice is a team product, and nobody has priced the team's share.
sparks.firstStep: Work with one estate of a deceased broadcaster to draft a trust schedule listing the five collaborators who shaped the signature delivery, and the percentage each would receive on a licensing deal.
